It requires law enforcement to proactively segregate evidence from non-public data, creating a predictable and accountable process. And it preserves full rule 16 disclosures. Every piece of electronic evidence required under rule 16 must still be turned over to the defense.

It creates a clear court process for the defense to request access if they believe directly related evidence is in the non-public data. And it mandates written policies within law enforcement and prosecutorial agencies to ensure sensitive data is used only for legitimate purposes and stored securely.

What this bill does not do, it does not limit any constitutional rights of the accused. All Utah and US constitutional protections remain fully intact, including Brady obligations. It does not restrict defense access to evidence.

Anything directly related to the charged crime must still be disclosed along with all exculpatory material. It does not create a newer burdensome discovery system. It works entirely through existing Rule 16 procedures.

It does not mirror victim veto systems in other states. It does not give victims or prosecutors the power to block discovery. It does not hinder defense attorneys. It actually helps them avoid ethical pitfalls by establishing clearer standards for handling sensitive materials.
